meta.title: The State of AI in Marketing: 2026
meta.subtitle: What the data actually says about adoption, impact, and the gap between the hype and the results.
meta.author: Dr. Aisha Khan

blocks.text: Adoption stories are easy to tell and hard to verify. We pulled the numbers from three independent surveys to separate what teams say from what they do — and where the impact is real.

blocks.title: What the data shows
items: 73% of teams use AI in at least one workflow
Most usage is shallow — one or two workflows
Deep, cross-functional adoption is where outsized returns cluster

blocks.alt: A chart of AI adoption over time
blocks.caption: Adoption crossed from early-adopter to default in under two years.

blocks.text: The headline number hides a wide spread. Self-reported impact runs ahead of measured impact; teams that instrument a single honest metric report smaller — but real — gains.

blocks.title: A caveat worth naming
blocks.body: Survey enthusiasm is not the same as measured ROI. The gap between the two is the story of 2026.

blocks.text: The technology is ahead of the measurement. The teams that close that gap are the ones that win.
blocks.source: — Dr. Aisha Khan, Marketing Science Group

meta.title: Does Remote Work Actually Work? The Data, Honestly
meta.subtitle: Productivity, retention, and the claims on both sides — measured against what the studies really found.
meta.author: Dr. Aisha Khan

blocks.text: Both camps cite studies. Both camps are partly right. We read the research that actually controlled for confounders and ignored the rest.

blocks.title: Findings that survive scrutiny
items: Focused individual work tends to improve remotely
Onboarding and weak ties suffer without intervention
Outcomes track management quality more than location

blocks.caption: Location explains less of the variance than management does.

blocks.text: The strongest finding is also the least convenient for both sides: the policy matters far less than the practices. Well-run teams do well anywhere.

blocks.title: Read the methods
blocks.body: Most viral remote-work statistics fail to separate the pandemic shock from steady-state remote work. Treat 2020-2021 data with care.

blocks.text: Location is a weak predictor. Management is a strong one. The debate aimed at the wrong variable.
blocks.source: — Dr. Aisha Khan, Marketing Science Group

meta.title: The Creator Economy, by the Numbers
meta.subtitle: Beyond the headlines about million-dollar influencers: what the broad middle of the creator economy actually earns.
meta.author: Dr. Aisha Khan

blocks.text: The headlines profile the top 1% and call it an economy. The data on the other 99% tells a more sober — and more useful — story.

blocks.title: What the numbers show
items: Earnings are extremely top-heavy and power-law shaped
The sustainable middle relies on diversified income
Platform dependence is the single biggest risk factor

blocks.alt: A chart of creator earnings distribution
blocks.caption: A long tail, a thin middle, and a famous few.

blocks.text: The creators who last are not the ones with the most followers. They are the ones who own a direct relationship with their audience and refuse to depend on a single platform.

blocks.title: The structural risk
blocks.body: An algorithm change can erase a business overnight. Owned channels — email, community — are the only real insurance.

blocks.text: Followers are rented. The relationship is the only thing you own.
blocks.source: — Dr. Aisha Khan, Marketing Science Group
